originalTitle: As Warsh and the Fed contemplate fewer meetings, markets brace for potential volatility ahead
summary: Since taking office in May, Warsh has implemented several measures that reverse decades of Fed culture.
content:
Add the possibility of fewer meetings into the mix of how Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh wants to reduce the central bank's footprint on financial markets, a move that some experts say could introduce both volatility and opportunity for investors.

Since taking office in May, Warsh has implemented several measures that reverse decades of Fed culture in which policymakers have been aggressively transparent — some say overly so — about where they think monetary policy is headed.

Thus far, he has curtailed so-called forward guidance, or how the Fed signals its future rate moves, dramatically shortened the postmeeting statement and provided cryptic and often evasive answers when questioned about his views during the two news conferences he's held so far.

Now comes the possibility, discussed in what one Fed source described as mostly hypothetical terms, of reducing the long-held schedule of eight meetings each year for the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee.

Such a move would further curtail the communications output from the Warsh Fed — and lead to some uncertain outcomes for the stock and bond markets.

"Certainly, it's going to increase volatility," said George Catrambone, head of fixed income for the Americas at DWS Group. "Having less transparency forces market participants to hedge or have a wider dispersion of outcomes."

The Fed has used various meeting strategies over the decades.

Until the early 1980s, it met nearly monthly before changing to eight a year under former Chairman Paul Volcker. Moreover, the Fed is free at any time to call a meeting, though the market implications could be substantial given that such a move would be considered an emergency.

Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari told CNBC on Wednesday that he is fine with reexamining the meeting schedule.

"I don't think there's any magic number about eight or 10 or six. You know, we always have the ability to call emergency meetings if things happen, but that's a big event," he said. "When the FOMC calls an emergency meeting, it really sends a signal that we're concerned about something. And so, you know, I think I'm open-minded. I don't have a strong view."

Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson on Tuesday expressed similar sentiments, telling CNBC, "It's healthy to have a good discussion about that." Other Fed experts take a similar tack that having a fewer meetings a year might not be a big deal to markets.

"There's nothing magical about eight meetings," said Bill English, the Fed's former head of monetary affairs during Warsh's first stint there and now a Yale professor. "There are costs associated with having a lot of meetings, but on the other hand, you don't want to have so few meetings that you end up not acting in a timely way."

English said he once proposed six meetings a year, but with each including a news conference as well as an update to the Fed's Summary of Economic Projections. Overall, he sees eight as "close to the right number" and instead is more concerned about other aspects of Warsh's strategy.

"I really don't like this effort to communicate much less," he said. "Explaining more about why you're doing what you're doing helps the public to understand it. It helps the public to anticipate it. It makes monetary policy more effective, and also it just seems like it's appropriate to make the Fed accountable."

So far, markets either have been willing to give Warsh the benefit of the doubt, or simply have been too focused on geopolitics to care about the Fed rumblings.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average has added about 3,500 points, or 7%, since Warsh took over from now-Governor Jerome Powell on May 22. Bond yields on net have risen, though not dramatically, with the policy-sensitive 2-year Treasury up about 8 basis points, or 0.08 percentage points, while the benchmark 10-year yield has risen about the same.

Those moves have come despite Warsh defying a tradition of open communication that dates back into the latter part of the 20th century while also establishing five task forces aimed at a top-to-bottom rethinking of the Fed's approach to policy, communications strategy and data utilization, among other things.

"He's kind of getting away with it," said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist at Nationwide. "Warsh is really the first Fed official that I've seen explicitly say he wants the Fed to have less direct impact on market movement."

Indeed, Warsh has told market participants explicitly that they should be reacting to data, not the vagaries of Fedspeak.

"Market participants are learning to play the ball, not the referee — and market prices will continue to respond in the direction and magnitude they see fit," Warsh said during last week's news conference. "This is, in my view, a change for the better — and we are just getting started."

Still, some investors think Warsh's strategy is risky.

"The main takeaway is more volatility," Dario Perkins, head of global macroeconomics at TS Lombard, said in a note in which he deemed the result of Warsh's approach "a regime of continuous market repricing."

"Investors have to get used to FOMC meetings at which they don't know the outcome ahead of time," he said. "That will also provide new trading opportunities. It goes without saying that this may well be what Warsh has wanted all along."

Concerns already have been raised about the chairman's feelings over forward guidance, and that has been exacerbated by a loosely defined reaction function — a delineation of the economic conditions that would cause the Fed to react. Warsh also has spoken critically about the Fed's "dot plot" of individual officials' rate expectations and declined to submit his own dot when the Federal Open Market Committee last updated the grid in June.

Adding to the information vacuum by only meeting, say, four or six times a year raises further concerns that a market that has for decades looked for cues from the Fed now will have to guess at policy.

chineseTitle: 随着沃什和美联储考虑减少会议，市场为未来潜在的波动做好准备
chineseSummary: 自五月上任以来，沃什实施了多项措施，扭转了美联储数十年的文化。
chineseContent:
美联储主席凯文·沃什希望减少央行在金融市场的影响，此外还可能减少会议次数，一些专家表示此举可能会给投资者带来波动和机会。

自五月上任以来，沃什实施了多项措施，扭转了美联储几十年来的文化，在这种文化中，政策制定者对货币政策的走向一直保持高度透明（有人说过于透明）。

到目前为止，他已经减少了所谓的前瞻性指引，即美联储如何暗示未来利率走势，大幅缩短了会后声明，并在迄今为止举行的两次新闻发布会上被问及他的观点时提供了含糊且常常回避的答案。

现在出现了一种可能性，一位美联储消息人士称，这种可能性主要是假设性的，即减少制定利率的联邦公开市场委员会每年举行八次会议的长期时间表。

此举将进一步削减沃什联储的通讯输出，并给股票和债券市场带来一些不确定的结果。

“当然，这会增加波动性，”DWS Group 美洲固定收益主管 George Catrambone 表示。 “透明度较低迫使市场参与者进行对冲或结果更加分散。”

几十年来，美联储使用了各种会议策略。

直到 20 世纪 80 年代初，该委员会几乎每月举行一次会议，后来在前主席保罗·沃尔克 (Paul Volcker) 的领导下改为每年八次。此外，美联储可以随时召开会议，尽管考虑到此举将被视为紧急情况，对市场的影响可能很大。

明尼阿波利斯联储主席尼尔·卡什卡利周三对 CNBC 表示，他同意重新审查会议日程。

“我不认为八、十或六有什么神奇的数字。你知道，如果发生事情，我们总是有能力召开紧急会议，但这是一个大事件，”他说。 “当联邦公开市场委员会召开紧急会议时，它确实发出了一个信号，表明我们对某些事情感到担忧。所以，你知道，我认为我是开放的。我没有强烈的观点。”

费城联储主席安娜·保尔森周二表达了类似的观点，她告诉 CNBC，“对此进行良好的讨论是有益的。”其他美联储专家也采取类似的策略，认为每年减少会议次数对市场来说可能不是什么大问题。

“八次会议并没有什么神奇之处，”沃什首次任职期间担任美联储货币事务主管、现任耶鲁大学教授的比尔·英格利希 (Bill English) 表示。 “召开大量会议会产生成本，但另一方面，你也不希望召开的会议太少，以致最终无法及时采取行动。”

英格利希表示，他曾提议每年举行六次会议，但每次会议都包括一次新闻发布会以及美联储经济预测摘要的更新。总的来说，他认为八个“接近正确的数字”，相反，他更关心沃什战略的其他方面。

“我真的不喜欢这种减少沟通的努力，”他说。 “更多地解释为什么要做你正在做的事情可以帮助公众理解它。它可以帮助公众预测它。它使货币政策更加有效，而且让美联储承担责任似乎是合适的。”

到目前为止，市场要么愿意相信沃什的说法，要么只是过于关注地缘政治而忽视了美联储的传言。

自沃什于 5 月 22 日接任现任州长杰罗姆·鲍威尔以来，道琼斯工业平均指数已上涨约 3,500 点，即 7%。债券净收益率有所上升，尽管幅度不大，其中政策敏感的 2 年期国债上涨了约 8 个基点，即 0.08 个百分点，而基准 10 年期国债收益率也上涨了大约相同的幅度。

尽管沃什违背了可以追溯到20世纪下半叶的开放沟通传统，同时还成立了五个工作组，旨在从上到下重新思考美联储的政策方法、沟通策略和数据利用等，但这些举措还是出现了。

Nationwide 首席市场策略师马克·哈克特 (Mark Hackett) 表示：“他似乎侥幸逃脱了惩罚。” “沃什确实是我见过的第一位明确表示希望美联储对市场走势减少直接影响的美联储官员。”

事实上，沃什已经明确告诉市场参与者，他们应该对数据做出反应，而不是对联邦言论的变幻莫测做出反应。

沃什在上周的新闻发布会上表示：“市场参与者正在学习如何打球，而不是裁判——市场价格将继续按照他们认为合适的方向和幅度做出反应。” “在我看来，这是一个更好的改变——而我们才刚刚开始。”

不过，一些投资者认为沃什的策略存在风险。

TS Lombard 全球宏观经济主管达里奥·珀金斯 (Dario Perkins) 在一份报告中表示，“主要的收获是波动性更大”，他认为沃什方法的结果是“一种持续的市场重新定价机制”。

“投资者必须习惯联邦公开市场委员会会议，他们无法提前知道会议结果，”他表示。 “这也将提供新的贸易机会。不用说，这很可能是沃什一直想要的。”

人们已经对主席对前瞻性指引的感受表示担忧，而松散定义的反应函数（对可能导致美联储做出反应的经济状况的描述）加剧了这种担忧。沃什还批评了美联储个别官员利率预期的“点阵图”，并在联邦公开市场委员会六月份上次更新网格时拒绝提交自己的点阵图。

每年只召开四到六次会议，进一步加剧了信息真空，这进一步引发了人们的担忧，即几十年来一直在寻找美联储线索的市场现在将不得不猜测政策。
